title: Agents and tool use: project 3
why: Employers are hiring for agentic systems, and interviewers probe judgement: when an agent helps and when a fixed workflow is safer and cheaper.
outcomes: Tell workflows from agents and choose deliberately
Design tools with clear names, descriptions and schemas
Run loops with step limits, error paths and approvals
Expose a tool through the Model Context Protocol
lessons: Read Building Effective Agents and map each pattern to a use case
Build a plain tool-calling loop without a framework
Give the agent three tools: your RAG search, a SQL query and one public API
Add guardrails: step limit, input validation, tool-failure handling, approval before risky actions
Expose one tool through an MCP server
Rebuild with LangGraph or a provider agent SDK; compare the complexity honestly
resources: IBM RAG and Agentic AI (agent courses)
method: Start with a workflow, and only promote it to an agent when you can name the decision the model has to make. Write that decision in the README.
build: Project 3: a deployed agent with decision logs, a step limit and a path for tool failure.

quiz.q: When should you not use an agent?
o: When the steps are known in advance; use a fixed workflow
quiz.e: Agents add cost and unpredictability. Use them only when the path depends on the model's decisions.

o: A name, a clear description and an input schema
quiz.e: The model picks tools from the description and fills arguments from the schema.

o: To stop endless loops and runaway cost
quiz.e: Unbounded loops are a common and expensive agent failure.

o: An open protocol for connecting models to tools and data sources
quiz.e: The Model Context Protocol standardises how tools and data are exposed to models.

o: To debug and explain what it did and why
quiz.e: Logs are how you diagnose a wrong tool choice and show reviewers your reasoning.
